Pantheon CI runs this on Linux, macOS and Windows against current hermes-agent, and all three fail in the test this PR adds:

```
FAILED tests/test_homeassistant_adapter_ported.py::TestConfigIntegration::test_env_override_creates_ha_platform
>       assert ha.token == "env-token"
E       AssertionError: assert None == 'env-token'
```

The original repo had no CI, so this is the first time it has run. The other 63 tests pass. @Bendak, could you take a look? Push fixes to this branch or open a new PR against `hermes-pantheon`.

Ran the suite on this branch against a hermes-agent checkout: 66 passed, 2 skipped, matching the PR description.

Two review points, neither blocking:

1. **Retry depends on matching HA's error text.** `"return_response" in body.lower()` breaks silently if HA rewords the 400 message. Forecast calls would then go back to failing with a plain 400 and no obvious cause. Consider asking HA which services support responses (`GET /api/services` lists a `response` flag per service) and caching that, or at minimum a comment at the call site naming the string as a known coupling.

2. **Response services always make two requests.** Because `_async_call_service` passes `return_response=True`, the plain attempt is always sent first for `weather.get_forecasts` and similar services. It's harmless, but the `/api/services` lookup in point 1 would remove the extra round trip too.

Minor: no test covers a 400 that doesn't mention `return_response` (should raise, not retry). A one-line test would pin that down.

Two more triggers for the same pattern, and a status check after the 9 Oct update. Plugin 0.3.3 (`4bc79c7`), Hermes v0.21.6+145 (main `d687605`), Claude Code 2.1.283, Opus 5.5 at high effort, Slack + Zulip gateway, 1 h cache TTL.

**Still happening.** Turn-start re-writes are 24-31% of all cache writes each day from 6 to 9 Oct, with no trend. Since the 9 Oct update, 32 of 81 turn starts re-wrote more than 20K tokens. Over 5 days, turn starts re-wrote 29.0M tokens that were already cached, which we estimate at about 13% of our weighted usage.

**Trigger 2: a mid-turn steer.** With `display.busy_input_mode: steer`, Hermes delivers a message that arrives mid-turn as a new user row after the latest tool result. That looks like a turn start to the cache, and after a long loop it misses the same way. One example, call 41 to 43 of a single turn:

```
API call NousResearch/hermes-plugin-claude-subscription-directsdk#41: in=177894 out=299  cache=176360/177894 (99%) write=1517
run_agent: Delivered /steer to agent after tool batch (381 chars) as new user message
API call NousResearch/hermes-plugin-claude-subscription-directsdk#42: in=178542 out=2676 cache=30568/178542 (17%) write=147956
API call NousResearch/hermes-plugin-claude-subscription-directsdk#43: in=184485 out=2883 cache=178524/184485 (97%) write=5944
```

The read falls back to about 30K, which is system plus tools only: the same "miss (tools+system only)" case as in the issue's table. The call after it hits again. We saw three of these since 6 Oct (147K, 79K and 56K re-written); this one came 41 calls into the turn. Steering is useful, so a fix that covers turn starts should cover this too, as long as the breakpoint logic treats any new user frame (not only the first one in a turn) as a turn boundary.

**Trigger 3, less certain: image results.** A few calls right after native-vision `vision_analyze` results or browser screenshots miss in the same way (5 large ones, 64-225K each; only 3 of 154 native-vision results missed). Unlike the steer case, the input shrinks by 2.5-4.7K tokens at the miss, for example:

```
API call NousResearch/hermes-plugin-claude-subscription-directsdk#55: in=213658 out=5480 cache=212430/213658 (99%) write=1211
(two vision_analyze results, native fast path)
API call NousResearch/hermes-plugin-claude-subscription-directsdk#56: in=209628 out=5310 cache=28297/209628 (13%) write=181314
API call NousResearch/hermes-plugin-claude-subscription-directsdk#57: in=212250 out=5074 cache=209611/212250 (99%) write=2622
```

So something earlier in the prefix changed, which may be a different cause (for example thinking dropped when images arrive in a user frame). We haven't captured the request bodies for this one, so treat it as a lead rather than a diagnosis.

Between the two, mid-turn misses since 6 Oct are small (about 0.3M tokens a day). The turn-start case is still the big one.

Data point from a second install, on a subscription login, where the `messages[1]` rewrite happens but `cache_read` does not freeze.

**Setup.** Arch Linux, Hermes `80852053`, plugin `31b591f` plus local diagnostics only (the opt-in prefix trace from NousResearch/hermes-plugin-claude-subscription-directsdk#33 and the two commits of NousResearch/hermes-plugin-claude-subscription-directsdk#89; no other change to `admission.py`). Claude Code moved from 2.1.291 to 2.1.293 during the window.

**Live traffic, 6 Oct 12:46 to 7 Oct 18:30.** The trace records per-message digests of what the relay forwards. In 17 sessions with at least three calls I can compare request 1 and request 2, and in all 17 native rewrote `messages[1]` exactly as described here: one text block on request 1, a plain string on request 2, plus a trailing `role: system` message. The model was Opus 5.5 in 10 of them, Sonnet 5.5 in 4 and Haiku 5.5 in 3. In 14, the first thinking block sits at `messages[2]`, right after the edited message. Even so, every transition from call 1→2 through call 4→5 read exactly the previous read plus write (deficit 0 in 68 of 68 transitions). Across all 1,543 consecutive call pairs in the window, no run of three calls has a frozen `cache_read`.

**Controlled, in the reporter's shape.** Throwaway `HERMES_HOME`, `terminal` as the only tool, the plugin at exactly `31b591f`, `CLAUDE_SUBSCRIPTION_DIRECTSDK_COMMAND` pointed at the 2.1.291 binary, `claude-sonnet-5[1m]`, one turn of 6 sequential tool calls and a resumed second turn of 3. I reproduced this offline with Claude Code 2.1.286 (real CLI, the plugin's relay, a fake loopback upstream). A few things that may help.

**What turns the title request on.** In the 2.1.286 bundle, native skips its session-title request when any of these holds:
- non-essential traffic is off (`CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC`);
- `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_TERMINAL_TITLE` is set;
- the entrypoint is `sdk-cli`, which `claude -p` sets when none is inherited, there is no `CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_VERSION` or `CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE_SESSION_ID`, and the server flag `tengu_quizzical_thimble` is on (its default).

So under `-p` it is normally off. It can come on when the Hermes process carries a `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT` other than `cli` or `sdk-cli`, or `CLAUDE_AGENT_SDK_VERSION` or `CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE_SESSION_ID`, which a gateway started from another Claude Code or Agent SDK process can inherit, or when that flag is off for the account. Some data for the design question, from building a similar guard in another Claude Code integration.

**The signal exists in-stream today; this plugin just drops it.** Claude Code 2.1.286 emits a `rate_limit_event` stream-json message whose `rate_limit_info` carries `rateLimitType`, `overageStatus` and `isUsingOverage`. `directsdk.py`'s receive loop only handles `assistant`, `result` and `stream_event`, so the event is discarded. A guard can't stop the request that reveals overage, because that request is already charged. The workable shape is the "policy before spawn" one you describe: record the signal, then refuse the next spawn.

**Pitfalls we hit:**
- **`overageStatus: "allowed"` only means overage is permitted, not in use.** Blocking on it stops subscribers who still have allowance. Only `isUsingOverage: true` (or `rateLimitType: "overage"`) means paid use.
- **`rateLimitType: "seven_day_overage_included"` is a subscription window** (the Fable allowance), alongside `five_hour`, `seven_day`, `seven_day_opus` and `seven_day_sonnet`. Treating every non-five-hour or non-seven-day value as paid blocks Fable wrongly.
- **A missing event is not evidence either way.** Failing closed on absence would block normal turns. Fail closed only in the strict-reserve mode you describe, and only once usage data is actually readable.

If you go in-plugin, the smallest version I'd suggest:
- An opt-in `block_extra_usage` setting, read per spawn like `claude_code_telemetry`.
- Remember the last time paid use was seen, with an expiry at the window's reset time.
- Report it in `native_admission`.
- Refuse the next spawn with a 402-style `ClaudeAPIError`, so Hermes takes its fallback.

If you'd rather have hooks, the same three facts are what the hook payload needs. Happy to send either once you pick the boundary.

Adding a second reason to fix this: under multiplex there is no safe way to scope the token at all, not just no way to pick between two accounts.

**What we see (Hermes 0.21.5, plugin 0.3.3 @ 682b22d, Linux container, `gateway.multiplex_profiles` on):**

- `__init__.py::_subscription_token()` and the spawn path in `directsdk.py` (`env = dict(self.env if self.env is not None else os.environ)`) read `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` only from the gateway **process** environment.
- A served profile's `.env` is deliberately not loaded into `os.environ` under multiplex (`hermes_cli/env_loader.py`, "skipping process-global dotenv load for routed profile home"), so a token in one profile's `.env` never reaches `claude`.
- The only way to make it work under one host gateway is to set `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` process-wide (container env, service `EnvironmentFile`, etc.).
- Core deliberately leaves `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` **off** the provider env scrub list (`tools/environments/local_env_policy.py`, `blocked.discard("CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN")`, see hermes-agent #55878). The reason is sound for a desktop user's own `claude` install. On a multiplexed gateway, though, a process-wide token is inherited by the terminal-tool children (and script runners) of **every** served profile, including profiles that never select this provider. Any agent shell on the host can read the subscription credential, including one steered by prompt injection from an inbound channel.

So today an operator who wants the subscription on one profile has to choose between process-wide exposure of the token to every profile's shells, or the `gateway.standalone` shim, which the docs mark as temporary.

**Proposal (extends the `claude_config_dir` setting suggested above):**

1. Resolve the credential **per profile at spawn time**: read `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` (and `CLAUDE_SUBSCRIPTION_DIRECTSDK_CONFIG_DIR` / the proposed `claude_config_dir` setting) through the active profile's secret scope (`agent.secret_scope.get_secret`, which is already contextvar-bound for the turn under multiplex), falling back to `os.environ` only when multiplex is off.
2. Inject the resolved value **only into the env dict passed to the spawned `claude` child** (and the `auth status` / `initialize` handshake children in `directsdk_setup.py`), never into `os.environ`.
3. Use the same per-profile resolution in `fetch_account_usage` for the `/usage` call.
4. Optionally declare `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` in `optional_env` so `hermes model` / setup can point users at the profile `.env`.

With that, an operator can put the token in one profile's `.env` and keep it out of the host process environment, so other profiles' shells never inherit it. The selected profile's own shells would still see it only if that profile also passes it through on purpose.

Thanks for porting this! Happy to help with the failing test — I dug into it, found the real mechanism, and prepared a minimal fix (details + validation below).

## Root cause

All three runners fail at the same assert — and the failure is narrower than it looks. The traceback shows the earlier asserts **passing**: the `homeassistant` platform **is** created and enabled in `load_gateway_config()` (the registry builds the entry via the plugin's `env_enablement_fn`), and `extra["url"]` is seeded from `HASS_URL` (verified locally — that assert sits after the failing one in the original test, so CI never reached it). What's `None` is only `ha.token`:

```
        assert Platform("homeassistant") in config.platforms   # passes
        assert ha.enabled is True                              # passes
>       assert ha.token == "env-token"
E       AssertionError: assert None == 'env-token'
```

What died with the core extraction (NousResearch/hermes-agent#132469) is the core credential row that copied `HASS_TOKEN` into `PlatformConfig.token`:

```diff
-    _Cred(Platform.HOMEASSISTANT, ("HASS_TOKEN",), token="HASS_TOKEN", optional=(("url", "HASS_URL"),)),
```

The plugin now owns that: its adapter reads the token from the env itself (`config.token or _get_scoped_secret("HASS_TOKEN", "")`). So the test asserts a token-propagation contract that core deliberately dropped.

## Fix

Keep everything that still passes; move the token assert to the layer that owns it now:

```python
        monkeypatch.setenv("HASS_TOKEN", "env-token")
        monkeypatch.setenv("HASS_URL", "http://10.0.0.5:8123")
        # Clear other platform tokens
        for v in ["TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN", "DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN", "SLACK_BOT_TOKEN"]:
            monkeypatch.delenv(v, raising=False)

        from gateway.config import PlatformConfig, load_gateway_config
        config = load_gateway_config()

        assert Platform("homeassistant") in config.platforms
        ha = config.platforms[Platform("homeassistant")]
        assert ha.enabled is True
        assert ha.extra["url"] == "http://10.0.0.5:8123"
        # Core no longer copies HASS_TOKEN into PlatformConfig.token (that
        # credential row left with the core extraction in
        # NousResearch/hermes-agent#132469); the
        # adapter reads the token from the env itself. Assert it at the layer
        # that owns it now:
        adapter = HomeAssistantAdapter(PlatformConfig(enabled=True))
        assert adapter._hass_token == "env-token"
```

## Validation

- The ported file (`test_homeassistant_adapter_ported.py`, 82 items) passes **82/82** with the fix, in a local hermes-agent environment (pytest venv, current core).
- CI counts for reference (whole `tests/` dir, 4 files / 147 items): macOS `1 failed, 145 passed, 1 skipped`; Ubuntu and Windows `1 failed, 144 passed, 2 skipped` — only the assert above fails on all three.
- One heads-up unrelated to this PR: `test_plugin_registration.py::TestPlatformRegistration::test_is_connected_requires_non_blank_hass_token` can fail on hosts that have a real `HASS_TOKEN` in their Hermes home `.env` — `monkeypatch.delenv` doesn't reach the scope-aware, `.env`-backed env reader, so `is_connected` still returns `True` there. It passes on clean CI runners; pre-existing, not introduced here.

Thanks for this — moving the routes off the event loop is exactly what large installs need. I applied the backend part of this PR locally (at head `a1650588`) on a Hermes v0.21.7 dashboard and ran it against a much larger, *live* dataset than the synthetic benchmark. Sharing measurements in case they help the review.

**Testbed (one machine, Windows 11, Python 3.14):** `state.db` = 1.79 GB, 1,115 sessions, 185,897 messages (~0.28 GB of message text), with a gateway writing to the DB continuously.

**Confirmed working:**
- With the five routes offloaded, the dashboard stays fully responsive *while* a cold overview aggregation runs: `/` returned in 1.7 ms and `/api/dashboard/plugins` in 6.8 ms, measured during the aggregation. Before this, the whole server was unresponsive for minutes. 
- The extraction-reuse logic and the new tests pass (40/40 local suite). Note: `test_real_host_selected_profile` XPASSes on host v0.21.7, which already scopes plugin routes for `?profile=` — the strict xfail just needs relaxing on newer hosts.

**Where large + active installs still hurt:**
- Overview / subject-detail / day-detail aggregation remains the dominant cost and stays uncached: cold overview ≈ 41 s in an isolated process, ~71 s in the live dashboard process. Every cold open recomputes everything — repeat opens pay it again.
- On an active install the stamp-based reuse rarely hits: `state.db` / `-wal` stamps change with every gateway write, so `_subject_index` rebuilds on essentially every request. Two consecutive `/subjects?limit=5` calls here took 15.4 s and 14.6 s (both full rebuilds). The 5 s TTL doesn't act as a fallback because reuse requires a stamp match even for entries younger than the TTL.

**Suggestions (take or leave):**
1. When the stamp differs but the entry is younger than the TTL, reuse it anyway — on an active WAL that trades at most a few seconds of search staleness for skipping a rebuild on every query.
2. A short-TTL result cache for the remaining uncached endpoints would remove the "every open is a cold open" behavior. (I added a small local 300 s result cache as a stopgap; warm hits ≈ 25 ms.)
3. Maybe note the active-database behavior in the README so the benchmark numbers aren't read as universal.

We ran `100yenadmin:warm-fixes-for-29` (`67fc442`) against the plugin as we run it today (0.3.3), on our own workload. Each mode ran in its own isolated HERMES_HOME through `hermes chat`, with Claude Code 2.1.296, `claude-sonnet-5-5[1m]` at medium effort, and compression off. The task is a chained 9-tool round (terminal, read_file, search_files, write_file, patch, an 8 s sleep, then read back). The reference padding is real Rails source, sized to the input per step. Runs were interleaved, n=3 per mode and size, with a fresh nonce per run. Every answer was checked against ground truth.

**Speed: warm halves step latency at every size.**

| input/step | mode | median wall | median step 2+ | step 1 | `claude` spawns | correct |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ~57k | per-call | 76.5 s | 5.7 s | 6.7 s | 10 | 3/3 |
| ~57k | warm | 48.5 s | 2.7 s | 6.0 s | 1 | 3/3 |
| ~140k | per-call | 86.9 s | 6.3 s | 8.4 s | 10 | 3/3 |
| ~140k | warm | 51.7 s | 3.0 s | 6.4 s | 1 | 3/3 |
| ~273k | per-call | 100.2 s | 6.6 s | 8.2 s | 10 | 3/3 |
| ~273k | warm | 62.8 s | 3.8 s | 9.8 s | 1 | 3/3 |

A 30-step run at ~140k gave the same result: median step 2+ was 6.1 s per-call and 3.3 s warm. There was one cold start per process, every other step reused, and no rebuild or kill happened mid-turn. The answer was correct in both modes. There were no errors, `unrestored` reports or denied admissions.

**Caching: warm writes the whole first turn twice.**

On a conversation's first turn, warm step 2 reads only the system and tools prefix (~4.8k) and writes the full history again:

| ~140k, 10 steps | cache writes per run | read share |
|---|---|---|
| per-call | 136k | 90.3% |
| warm | 269k | 81.0% |

The pattern is the same at ~57k (53k vs 104k) and ~273k (269k vs 535k). In the 30-step run the only difference was step 2 (+133k). After that, warm reads at the same rate as per-call.

Cause: `_frame_first` (the #77 fix) runs on warm steps too, and its premise does not hold for a warm process. We dumped each request after `pin_message_breakpoint`:

- Request 1. Native sends `[<system-reminder>, <Hermes frame>]` as user message 0. `_frame_first` moves the reminder after the frame, and the request goes out as `[frame, reminder]`.
- Request 2, per-call. A fresh native replays message 0 without the reminder, so `[frame]` is a prefix and the cache hits. This is what #77 is for.
- Request 2, warm. The same live process replays message 0 exactly as it first built it: `[reminder, frame]`. `_frame_first` no longer applies, because an assistant message now exists. Message 0 therefore differs from what was cached at request 1, and the prefix breaks at its first block.

Check: we ran the same branch code with only the `_frame_first` call skipped for warm, in a scratch copy and nowhere else. On the 3-tool probe, warm step 2 then read 54,859 of 54,861 tokens (100%) with no second write. Step 1 was unchanged: it read 4.8k and wrote 50k. On the 30-step ~140k run, turn-1 writes dropped from 270.7k to 136.2k, the same as per-call. Median step 2+ was 2.9 s and the answer was correct.

Suggested fix: when the relay serves a warm session, skip the first-turn reorder, for example with `Admission(..., reorder_first=False)` from `_warm_spawn`. Or apply it on every warm request, so that native's order is rewritten the same way each time. We used the skip. It costs nothing on step 1, as measured above. The extra write happens once per warm process. A `--resume`d turn (a new Hermes process) starts cold. This matches #26. Claude Code sends its own session-title request during a turn, and `{"title": "..."}` is that request's answer. The plugin's relay admits exactly one upstream request per step. When the title request gets there first, it takes the step: its JSON comes back as the reply, and the real turn's request is denied. Whether Claude Code sends the title request depends on the environment it inherits and on a server-side feature flag for the account. That's why it shows up on some setups and not others, and why Hermes' own title generator setting doesn't affect it.

Until #26 is merged and the catalog pin moves, either of these stops it:
- **Recommended:** add `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_TERMINAL_TITLE=1` to the gateway's environment.
  - For a systemd user service, put `Environment=CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_TERMINAL_TITLE=1` in the unit or a drop-in, run `systemctl --user daemon-reload`, then restart the service.
  - The plugin passes the gateway's environment through to Claude Code.
- **Or:** set the plugin's `claude_code_telemetry` setting to `false`.
  - This turns off Claude Code's non-essential traffic, including the title request.
  - It also turns off its feature-flag fetch, so the model picker may list fewer models.

#26 tested this offline against the real Claude Code (2.1.286 and 2.1.292):

- with the fix: no title requests and nothing denied.

**Warm mode on Opus 5.5: benchmark results so far, plus one fix pushed (20098b7)**

Setup: Opus 5.5 (`claude-opus-5-5[1m]`), effort high, Claude Code 2.1.292/2.1.299, pinned Hermes `71d34bad`, this PR's head plus a bench-only usage log. All dollar figures are list-price equivalents computed from the upstream usage of each request. None of them is a subscription-meter reading.

**Pushed: `20098b7`, warm user-idle default 600 s → 3600 s.** Native writes its prompt cache with a 1-hour TTL, so a user-idle session should live for that hour. Until now, a reply that came 10–60 minutes after the last answer found its session reaped. The respawned native then replayed the history and wrote part of it to cache again, although the cached copy was still live. Both defaults stay below native's 3,900 s `clear_tool_uses` idle trigger, and the pool cap still bounds residency.

**Single-turn, warm vs per-call (15 matched pairs: 3 task families × 5 seeds):**
- **Runner wall time:** warm was lower in 15/15 pairs, 0.72× (95% CI 0.64–0.81).
- **List cost:** no clear difference on this mix: 0.97× by geometric mean (95% CI 0.89–1.05). That does not show the costs are equal.
  - By task: reasoning-heavy 0.78× (cheaper in 5/5), file chores 1.10×, bug fix 1.06×.
  - Warm generated less thinking (−$0.128 across pairs) but wrote more to cache (1.12×; +$0.080). That includes a constant +187 cache-write tokens at warm's second request in 15/15 pairs, a candidate for a small follow-up.
- **Within a user turn:** per-call still gets full cache hits across fresh processes.

**Between user turns: the bigger lever.** When a turn's steps produced thinking, per-call mode re-read the cache only up to the end of the previous turn's *first* request at the next user turn. Everything written after that was written again (6/6 boundaries). A warm session kept alive missed nothing (0/6); a warm session restarted between turns missed every time (6/6). Those prompts were small (~8–10k tokens). In a long session the re-write grows with each turn's tool output, so this looks related to #36. I'm now logging per-block request digests (hashes only) to find the first block that differs at the boundary.

**Multi-turn results on Opus 5.5, and the per-call turn-boundary cause**

Setup is the same as my previous comment: Opus 5.5 at high effort, Claude Code 2.1.299, pinned Hermes. Each conversation is 4 user turns with a 20 s pause between turns. Task mt1 ran on seeds 7500–7503, and every run passed its graders. Costs are list-price equivalents computed from upstream usage. They are not subscription-meter readings.

Ratios are list cost against headless Claude Code (`claude -p`, one process) on the same seeds, as geometric means over pairs:

| Mode | vs Claude Code | Cache misses at user-turn boundaries |
|---|---|---|
| Per-call | 1.115× (n=4) | 3 of 3 per conversation |
| Warm, kept alive between turns | 0.769× (n=4) | 0 |
| Warm, restarted every turn (old 600 s default with replies slower than 10 min) | 0.962× (n=4) | 3 of 3 |

- **Warm idle limit:** `20098b7` raises the default user-idle limit from 600 s to 3600 s. A session waiting on a human reply now stays in the pool as long as its prompt cache lives (1 h TTL), and stays below native's 3,900 s `clear_tool_uses` trigger.
- **Per-call misses at every user turn:** I diffed per-block hashes of consecutive upstream requests. Per-call native moves today's date line (`Today's date is YYYY-MM-DD.`) out of the environment system message into a trailing `role: system` message. On a new user turn it also puts its context reminder ahead of the newest user frame. Neither appears in the next request, which has two effects:
  - Each step's signed thinking is replayed without the context it was generated against, so Opus re-derives it (#40).
  - The cache entry from the previous turn's later steps stops matching (#36).
- **Fix, measured with a bench-only version of it:** the relay puts the date line back where native's opening request had it (the env block hash then matches the opening request exactly) and drops the reminder before the newest frame. Native's own tool-result steps already omit that reminder. Results with the fix:
  - per-call boundary misses fell from 3/3 to 0/3;
  - thinking fell from 3.2k/5.9k to 0.7k/1.8k tokens;
  - list cost fell to 0.68× the unfixed per-call runs, which is 0.78× Claude Code (n=2, mt1 seeds 7500–7501).
  - Per-call then costs about the same as warm kept alive.
- **Product version:** it is per-call only and independent of this PR, so it is a separate PR: #83. Warm requests skip it.

In a 10-turn smoke run, per-call re-wrote 48.9k and 28k tokens at turn boundaries across the two conversations. That is what the fix removes.

## Summary for reviewers: Hermes + Opus 5.5 vs Claude Code, what we measured and what we fixed

This comment replaces my two earlier comments, which I've hidden as outdated. Everything is here in one place.

### ELI5

This PR adds an opt-in **warm mode**: one Claude Code process stays alive per conversation, instead of a fresh process for every request (per-call, which stays the default).

Claude keeps a **prompt cache**. Re-reading a conversation it has already seen costs about 1/20th of the normal input price, but only if the start of the request matches what it saw before, byte for byte. The plugin broke that match in two places, so Hermes kept paying to re-write conversations that Claude Code doesn't re-write.

1. **Warm mode reaped its process too early.** `20098b7` corrects this inside this PR. The idle process was killed after 10 minutes, but the cache lives for an hour. So a reply that came 10–60 minutes later started over and re-wrote the conversation. The idle limit is now an hour.
2. **Per-call mode moved things around on every request** (fixed in #83). Each fresh Claude Code process moves today's date line and a context reminder to a new spot. So at every new user message, the whole conversation was written to the cache again, and Opus redid reasoning it had already done. #83 keeps both in a fixed place.

**What it costs with the fixes** (list prices: what the same usage would cost at Anthropic's published API prices, not what the subscription charges):
- **Over 10-turn conversations:**
  - Warm Hermes costs about the same as Claude Code (1.005×).
  - Per-call with #83 costs 0.96–1.03×.
  - Unfixed per-call costs 1.26×.
- **By task:**
  - On the coding task, Hermes costs about 1.15–1.3× Claude Code, because Hermes makes 2–4× more tool calls.
  - On the reasoning task, it costs about 0.8×.

**Restarts, fixed since (Oct 15):** when a warm session restarts (a reply after more than an hour, pool eviction, or a Hermes restart), its first turn used to re-write the conversation (row E below; #84). This PR's head now fixes that. A restarted process rebuilds the same request bytes as a kept-alive one: its context relocation, and its tool results in the MCP block shape. One more piece lands with #83: the restarted native splits the date line out, and #83's `stable_request_context` moves it back. In a pre-registered re-run on a build with both, a warm session restarted at every turn missed **0 of 36** user-turn boundaries and cost **0.99×** a kept-alive one ("Oct 15 re-run" below).

**Merging.** The two PRs can merge in either order, but #83 first is simpler: this PR's rebase then adds the small warm extension to its `stable_request_context`. They conflict in three small hunks, and I've built and tested the combination: #79 + #83 passes the full plugin suite with warm off and on (324 tests).
- **`admission.py`:** keep both. The relay must call #83's `stable_request_context` before #79's warm-aware `pin_message_breakpoint(..., gate.first_turn)`, the same order #83 uses.
- **`README.md`:** keep #79's "Canonical history" paragraph, add #83's per-call paragraph above it, and drop main's older copy.

I'll push the rebase for whichever merges second.

Heads-up for the rebase onto current main: #25 now interacts with main's per-profile `claude_config_dir` (`apply_config_dir`).

**The problem:** `settle_login` reaps the refresh lock using the raw `env`, then runs `/usage` with `_child_env(env)`, which applies the profile setting. Suppose the setting picks directory P while an inherited `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` points at Q. The reap looks in Q, so the stale lock in P survives, and the probe then runs in P with the lock still there. Per-request spawns are fine: there `apply_config_dir(env)` runs before `reap_orphaned_refresh_lock(env)`.

**What I ran locally** (merged main + #25 + #30 + #32):

```python
def settle_login(resolved, env, timeout):
    child = _child_env(env)  # the profile's config dir outranks an inherited one: reap where the probe looks
    reap_orphaned_refresh_lock(child)
    try:
        subprocess.run(resolved + ["-p", "/usage"], env=child, ...)
```

**Regression test** (fails without the fix):

```python
def test_the_lock_is_reaped_in_the_profile_directory_the_probe_uses(profile, tmp_path):
    from test_directsdk_config_dir import _set_config_dir
    command, env, config, log = _setup(tmp_path, expires_in=3600, lock=120)
    inherited = tmp_path / "inherited"
    inherited.mkdir()
    env["CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR"] = str(inherited)
    _set_config_dir(str(config))
    profile.setup_status(command=command, env=env)
    assert _calls(log)[0] == {"event": "usage", "lock": False}
    assert not (config / ".oauth_refresh.lock").exists()
```

**One more merge fix:** `test_setup_probes_pass_the_profile_directory` needs its probe counts raised by one (2 for `setup_status`, 3 for discovery), because `settle_login` runs its `/usage` first.

Follow-up evidence from using this branch end to end on a real install, in case it helps review. Entity and area names below are generalised, and the example is a simplified composite of what I saw rather than a verbatim transcript.

## An example of the failure this fixes

Request: "turn off the kitchen lights". The Kitchen area holds three lights: `light.ceiling_1`, `light.hood_1` and `light.hall_1` (named "Hall Switch 1"). A fourth, `light.kitchen_counter` ("Kitchen counter light"), is assigned to the *Living Room* area.

Before (area filter available, but the model chose `name`):

```
ha_list_entities(domain="light", name="kitchen")
→ light.kitchen_counter  (area: Living Room)   ← wrong room, matched on its name
→ light.ceiling_1        (area: Kitchen)
  (light.hood_1 and light.hall_1 not returned: their names don't contain "kitchen")
```

The model then switched the counter light and left the others alone.

After (this PR's description text):

```
ha_list_entities(domain="light", area="kitchen")
→ light.ceiling_1, light.hood_1, light.hall_1   (each with "area": "Kitchen")
```

## Measurements (`claude-haiku-5-5`, dry-run wording, exact entity set scored)

| Scenario | Without this PR | With this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Kitchen, 2 phrasings | 6/16 correct, `area` used in 5 | 10/10, `area` used in 10 |
| Two other rooms, 2 phrasings | not measured | 8/8, `area` used in 8 |

## A second finding: entity names still matter

With selection fixed, real (non-dry-run) requests still stopped short on two of the three lights. Their friendly names read like appliance switches ("... Oven Switch 1", "... Hall Switch 1") even though they are `light.*` entities that the area filter returned. The model reasoned, sensibly, that switching something called an oven switch might not be safe, and asked instead of acting. In all 4 real runs it left at least one of the two lights alone and asked about it (in one of them it did switch the other).

After renaming those two lights in Home Assistant to "... Light", real on and off requests both acted on all three lights with no questions (2 of 2 real runs; dry-run 10/10).

I deliberately did **not** try to word the descriptions to override that caution. For anything that sounds like an appliance, the right fix is a clear name, and that is a documentation point rather than code. If maintainers want it, a line in the README (area-based room requests, and naming light entities as lights) would cover it.

## One observation for later (not in this PR)

`ha_list_entities` also returns entities the registry marks as hidden. A "switch shown as light" helper hides its source switch, but that switch still shows up in `/api/states`, so the model sometimes sends the same command twice (`light.turn_off` and `switch.turn_off`). The registry data this PR already fetches includes the hidden flag, so skipping hidden entities in listings would be a small follow-up if you think it's worth it.

Limits: one install, one model, small samples. Treat it as a signal, not proof.

## Follow-up: practical Meshy asset + cinematic lessons for the skill

Separate from the feature suggestions above, these are reusable lessons from our saved Blender/game/cinematic workflows. They would fit well in optional references linked from `skills/meshy-3d/SKILL.md`—for example `blender-animation-handoff.md` and `cinematic-preflight.md`—rather than expanding the main skill into an entire production manual. These are downstream handling recommendations, not newly executed tests of this PR or universal defects in Meshy output.

### Model intake and preservation
- **Inspect before modifying.** Inventory the actual meshes, materials, UVs, texture dependencies, armatures, Actions, units and transforms. Preserve the original download and a versioned working copy. Don't remesh, rerig or reset transforms just because the import looks unfamiliar; protect an already working skin/rest pose and any artist-edited bones.
- **Decimation is purpose-specific.** A static background prop and an animated hero need different budgets. Keep the high-detail master; check the reduced version's silhouette, thin parts, UVs/materials and—if skinned—deformation in representative poses. Don't present a successful modifier/save as proof of quality. Check packed/external textures after reopening, not just in the original session.

### Animation imports: avoid “one character per clip” chaos
- **Treat repeated rig+mesh imports as clip carriers.** Inspect each clip on its original working pair first, choose one canonical performer, and retain the others as protected source carriers outside the active shot. An animation-only armature isn't a reason to rebind the canonical mesh blindly. Don't delete the only working source before verifying consolidation.
- **Matching bone names do not prove compatibility.** Compare hierarchy, full rest transforms, bone orientation/roll and object scale before reusing an Action. If they differ, retarget/bake a target-specific copy instead of assigning foreign local rotations. Some imported glTF rigs depend on non-identity pose-bone bases; indiscriminately zeroing them can break a healthy import. Don't edit bind/rest data merely to make bone displays look tidier.
- **Keep an actual animation library.** Give Actions stable, descriptive names; record source IDs, frame range, FPS, loop/root-motion status and target rig. Protect retained Actions from being discarded when unused (Fake User where appropriate). On slot-based Blender versions, assign the compatible Action slot as well as the Action. Reopen and play the result before retiring carriers. Recheck scene FPS after FBX imports; importing can change it.

### Cinematic assembly
- **Separate the library from the film.** Save a new cinematic `.blend` before adding cameras, NLA sequencing, lights or effects. Preserve live unsaved work and artist placement; never write a background-generated replacement over their active source. Changing look-dev should use reversible material copies, not destroy the approved textures.
- **Separate body motion, travel and camera movement.** Keep skeletal Actions reusable; use an explicit placement/motion root for world travel when appropriate. First measure existing root motion so it isn't applied twice. Accumulate travel across clips instead of snapping back to origin. Verify facing against travel direction, planted-foot behavior and actual deformed-mesh floor clearance—not just the rig origin.
- **Inspect clip edges and every loop seam.** Imported clips can contain bind-pose lead-ins, dead frames or recovery tails. Trim presentation strips, not protected source Actions. Preserve exact/fractional source endpoints when retiming. Review consecutive frames around NLA joins and repeat boundaries; maintain a reviewed baseline pose in gaps so the character doesn't flash into a T-pose. One good middle frame is not a playback test.
- **Attach props/VFX to evaluated animation.** Derive hand, weapon and muzzle positions from the final evaluated pose in world space, then inspect contact and visibility. Keep rigid accessories rigid where intended. Key effect-light energy off outside its beat; hiding or scaling the visible effect alone is not enough. Judge readability from the actual shot camera at delivery size, not only a close-up editor view.

### Approval, performance and delivery
- **Viewport choreography first, representative stills second, full render last.** Review the full unfamiliar retarget before batching more clips. Check camera framing, hands/feet, props and transition frames. For ensembles, being present in the Outliner doesn't mean a performer is recognizably visible. Optimize distant/static actors separately from the hero and compare both stills and motion before accepting the savings.
- **Make expensive renders recoverable.** Benchmark representative heavy frames, explain the estimated duration and get approval. Prefer numbered image sequences for restart/selective rerender, then encode a shareable derivative. For full-song work, extend choreography, secondary performers and cameras through the audio—not just the scene end marker. Verify final video FPS/duration/frame count/audio plus visual coverage and loop/transition seams.

A useful closing rule for the skill: report **downloaded**, **reopened/import-validated**, **visually reviewed**, **artist-approved**, and **tested in the target engine/render** as different states. None automatically implies the next.

— Mike, with Hermes-assisted workflow notes

Live check on real Claude (Opus 5.5, Claude Code 2.1.304), with hermes-agent#124566 and #31 applied: this PR's liveness chunks work, but for tool calls they reach Hermes too late to help on their own.

Timing every chunk the plugin's `Client` yields while Opus writes one 2,000-word `write_file` argument: 3,742 liveness chunks, all arriving in one burst at 93 s, after an 89.8 s gap. A real `hermes chat` run with a 30 s stall timer was killed.

The cause is upstream of this diff. Claude Code enables fine-grained tool streaming only when it talks to Anthropic directly. Behind our loopback relay, tools go out without `eager_input_streaming`, so the API buffers the whole argument. `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FINE_GRAINED_TOOL_STREAMING` did not add the flag (wire capture).

With the relay adding `eager_input_streaming: true` to each tool in the upstream body, the same call streams with no gap over 0.5 s, and the real `hermes chat` run completed: a 4,516-word file written in 111 s under the 30 s timer.

So this PR stays right, but the fix needs that relay change too. During thinking, this PR's chunks already arrive about every 1.2 s with display omitted, so the thinking half works as is.

Your measurement settles it: the approach in this PR cannot work, so I am parking it (marking this a draft) rather than keeping it in the review queue.

The two rows show the heuristic failing in both directions, and the reason is exactly what you say: Claude Code does not relay the upstream's pings - it emits its own about every 10 s, and none at all when the upstream goes fully silent. So a ping inside an open thinking block cannot tell thinking from stuck:

- a healthy silent think (12 s, then the answer) is killed at 6.3 s, before Claude Code's own first ping arrives - my change made the healthy case *worse* than main, not just unchanged;
- a stuck mid-think with the upstream pinging is never killed, because Claude Code's own pings keep arriving and the open thinking block counts them as progress.

Counting pings as progress is the only signal available here, and it is not a signal about the upstream at all. The signal that would work is the upstream's own progress, which needs the thinking stream to be visible - your #32 (request summarized thinking display).

So: parked behind #32, with no further changes from me until the thinking display is in. #60 is the superseded original of this rebase and I am closing it; if the watchdog work is picked up again it should start from the visible-thinking signal rather than from a ping heuristic.

**Verdict: request changes.** The Linux path is sound and the release layout the skill relies on is real, but the untested macOS step can write over a user's existing Blender. That's one sentence to fix, and the other changes below are small.

## Findings

1. **blocker: `blender/skills/blender/SKILL.md:47`: macOS can `ditto` over an existing `/Applications/Blender.app`.**
   The text leaves this to the agent's judgment ("already holds an older Blender the user **may** want to keep"). `ditto` does not replace a bundle. It merges into it. The old version's files (e.g. `Contents/Resources/4.x/`) stay, and the bundle's code seal is broken. On macOS 13+, App Management protection also stops a terminal or agent process from changing another app's bundle unless it has that permission. That can leave a half-written app. And the user never agreed to replace their Blender.
   Fix: never write into an existing `Blender.app`. If `/Applications/Blender.app` exists (any version), use `~/Applications/Blender.app`. If that also exists, stop and ask. Simplest of all: always install to `~/Applications` (see 2).

2. **should-fix: `SKILL.md:41`, `README.md:20`: on macOS the consent text says something untrue.**
   The question promises "their own user folders without administrator rights". On macOS the default target is `/Applications`, which is shared by every account on the Mac, and only admin-group users can write to it. Fix: install to `~/Applications/Blender.app` on macOS (it is already in the find list). That makes the promise true and removes finding 1. Otherwise, name `/Applications` in the question.

3. **should-fix: `SKILL.md:46`: the Linux `~/.local/bin/blender` link can shadow the user's own `blender`.**
   "Unless that path already exists" only protects the link path itself. Take a user who has an older distro Blender (`/usr/bin/blender`) or the snap (`/snap/bin/blender`), which is exactly the case that leads to this install. Ubuntu's `~/.profile` puts `~/.local/bin` ahead of both on `PATH`. After the install, typing `blender` in their shell runs the new 5.x. The question never mentioned that change.
   Two smaller gaps:
   - `ln -s` fails when `~/.local/bin` does not exist. Add `mkdir -p`.
   - A freshly created `~/.local/bin` only joins `PATH` at the next login. The MCP server inherits Hermes's `PATH`, so "so the `_for_cli` tools find it" is not guaranteed.

   Fix: create the link only when `command -v blender` finds nothing. Afterwards, re-check `command -v blender`. If it still finds nothing, tell the user the `_for_cli` tools need `PATH` and point to `references/setup.md`.

4. **should-fix (needs a matching hermes-agent change): the catalog still pins 0.3.0, and its disclosure becomes wrong.**
   `plugin-catalog/blender.yaml` on hermes-agent main pins `e9910ad` (0.3.0). Until it is repinned, `hermes plugins install blender` still refuses without Blender. Catalog presence (`hermes_cli/plugin_catalog_presence.py`) reads `plugin.json` at the pinned sha, so the badge only changes after the repin. The current description says Hermes "refuses the install when it is missing", and its `Disclosure —` sentence says nothing about downloading and installing a roughly 400 MB Blender. The repin PR must rewrite both.
   Also, the PR body's claim "Nothing else read that block for this plugin" is not accurate. That block was also read by:
   - `tools/mcp_tool_handlers.py` `_declared_app_offerable` (check_fn), which hid the tools when Blender was missing or older than 5.1 on macOS/Windows;
   - `tools/tool_search_catalog.py` `hidden_declared_sources`, the "hidden because…" note;
   - `tui_gateway/methods_tools_plugin_servers.py`, the Desktop server state sentence;
   - `plugin_catalog_presence.presence`, the onboarding/catalog "needs Blender" badge.

   After the repin, each of these falls back to "offerable" or `unknown`. That suits this design, because the skill now does the version check and the install. But the PR body should say so, so nobody restores the block expecting only an install-time effect. MCP startup is unchanged, as the body says.

5. **nit: `SKILL.md:44,48`: timeouts and Windows extraction speed.**
   The 270–410 MB download can outlast the `terminal` tool's 180 s default foreground timeout on a slower link. In Windows PowerShell 5.1, `Expand-Archive` on this zip (7.5k files, 0.95 GB) is slow because of its per-file progress output. Fix: tell the agent to run the download and extraction with a long timeout (or in the background and poll). On Windows, prefer `tar -xf <zip> -C "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\Blender Foundation"` (bsdtar ships with Windows 10 1803+ and 11), or set `$ProgressPreference='SilentlyContinue'` first. The resulting path is as documented (verified below).

6. **nit: `SKILL.md:47`: unreliable `hdiutil` mount point.**
   The mount point is `/Volumes/Blender`, or `/Volumes/Blender 1` when a volume of that name is already mounted, and the agent has to parse it out of a table. Use `hdiutil attach -nobrowse -readonly -mountpoint "<scratch>/blender-dmg" <file>` so the path is known and safe to quote.

7. **nit: `SKILL.md:41-49`: a failure leaves partial state behind.**
   "A step fails → link and stop" can leave a half-extracted `~/.local/opt/blender-*` or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\Blender Foundation\blender-*`. The find step's glob then picks it up next time. A download that fails the hash check also stays in scratch. Fix: extract into a scratch folder, move it into place only once complete, and delete the download whatever the outcome.

8. **nit: `SKILL.md:43`: "newest" needs to be numeric.**
   Text sorting gets this wrong: `Blender5.10/` would sort before `5.9/`, and `5.2.10` before `5.2.9`. The index also holds `Blender2.56abeta/`-style folders. Say: only `Blender<digits>.<digits>/`, compared numerically.

9. **nit: `SKILL.md:41`: the port warning reaches the question only indirectly.**
   The question pulls in the add-on's warning (runs Python as the user, port 9876 has no password) by pointing at another section. The live run carried it over, but write it straight into the install question so it can't be dropped.

10. **nit: integrity, not authenticity.**
    The `.sha256` file comes from the same host as the download, so it catches corruption and truncation, not a compromised mirror. The docs word this correctly. An optional cheap extra: `codesign --verify --deep --strict` on the app (macOS) and `Get-AuthenticodeSignature` on `blender.exe` (Windows) before first launch.

## Root cause found + working patch (Hermes v0.22.5, camofox plugin 1.0.0)

**Symptom as reported:** `browser_navigate` returns a snapshot, then every following
`browser_snapshot` / `browser_click` / `browser_type` in a later tool call returns
`{"success": false, "error": "No browser session. Call browser_navigate first."}`

**What I measured:** nine distinct user ids minted under one unchanged `sessionKey`
(`task_local-510cf6e3c4`) inside a ~12-minute window — e.g. `hermes_1ecd277543`,
`hermes_2f1c89e59d`, `hermes_78b2d175a0`, `hermes_4e80ee197e`, `hermes_f91b0d0df3`, with further ids
interleaved between those five. No `DELETE /sessions/...` appears inside that window, so nothing was
tearing the session down mid-sequence: each call simply asked for a *different* user. (DELETEs do
occur at other moments — 28 of them on this host that day — which is the lifecycle caveat at the end.)

**Cause:** `camofox_client.py` keeps `_sessions` in process memory, keyed by `(home_key, task_id or "default")`.
In my environment each tool call begins with that map empty — calls sharing one key produced a new
random id every time (nine ids, one key), which is only possible if the lookup missed on each call. `get_session` therefore
falls through to the ephemeral branch, which mints
`identity = {"user_id": f"hermes_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:10]}", ...}`.
A random id per call means the tab created by call N is invisible to call N+1 — the server still
holds it, but under a different user id. Nothing is actually broken server-side.

Scope note for maintainers: the map is process-local, so this reproduces wherever calls do not share
that process (a fresh worker per call, a module re-import, a CLI invocation per step). If your setup
dispatches tools in the same process the map would persist and the bug would not appear — the patch
below is correct either way, and the deterministic id also makes the failure impossible rather than
topology-dependent.

**Fix (+10/−2, one hunk, 5 effective code lines):** derive the id from `(state dir, task_id)` instead of
`uuid4`, so every call in the same task resolves to the same user, and adopt the existing tab.
Unkeyed calls keep a random id on purpose, so they never collapse onto one shared profile.
Note that tab adoption also needs `browser.camofox.adopt_existing_tab: true` (or
`CAMOFOX_ADOPT_EXISTING_TAB=1`); with that flag off the identity fix keeps the same user id but
starts a fresh tab, so a session that needs its prior page must set it.

```diff
--- a/camofox_client.py
+++ b/camofox_client.py
@@ -308,8 +308,16 @@
         if identity is None and _managed_persistence_enabled(camofox_cfg):
             identity = get_camofox_identity(key[1])
         if identity is None:
-            identity = {"user_id": f"hermes_{uuid.uuid4().hex[:10]}", "session_key": f"task_{key[1][:16]}"}
-            managed, adopt = False, False
+            # Task-scoped, not profile-scoped: derived from (this profile, this task) so a separate
+            # process finds the same browser again. Unkeyed calls keep a random id so they never
+            # collapse onto one shared profile.
+            digest = (uuid.uuid5(uuid.NAMESPACE_URL, f"camofox-task:{get_camofox_state_dir()}:{task_id}").hex[:10]
+                      if task_id else uuid.uuid4().hex[:10])
+            identity = {"user_id": f"hermes_{digest}", "session_key": f"task_{key[1][:16]}"}
+            # Adoption only makes sense for a reproducible identity: an unkeyed call just minted a
+            # random userId, so there can be no earlier tab. Skip the extra GET /tabs on that path.
+            managed, adopt = False, (bool(task_id) and
+                                     _flag("CAMOFOX_ADOPT_EXISTING_TAB", camofox_cfg, "adopt_existing_tab"))
         else:
             managed, adopt = True, _flag("CAMOFOX_ADOPT_EXISTING_TAB", camofox_cfg, "adopt_existing_tab")
         session = {"user_id": identity["user_id"], "tab_id": None, "session_key": identity["session_key"],
```

Applying it to the pristine plugin file (plugin v1.0.0) reproduces a file whose sha256 is
`7c7e952fc098938819cd7ed270408a8b4eeaed0099523871f5b322e8ebd66be9`; reversing the patch returns the
original `72e458eb9a9c5206...`, so the diff is exact and reversible.

**Verification:** a 10-check harness in which every step runs in a *separate OS process* (which is what
reproduces the defect) — navigate, snapshot, type, click and post-click, each in its own interpreter —
scores the unpatched plugin 5/10, failing the same-task identity check *and* the cross-process
snapshot, type, click and post-click checks, and 10/10 with the patch. That harness is local, not part
of the repo; I can paste it in full or turn it into a test file if useful. Live afterwards: navigate ->
snapshot -> type -> click -> snapshot across separate calls shows the typed value posted back
(`"custname": "arena"`), and one user id is reused for the whole call sequence.

**Caveat / open question for maintainers:** the plugin also registers an `on_session_end` hook
(`__init__.py:74-82`) that calls `cleanup_task` -> `close_session` -> `DELETE /sessions/{userId}`.
Hermes documents that hook as per-turn (`hermes_cli/lifecycle.py:72`: "`on_session_end` is per-turn and
stays observer-only"), while the plugin comment above it says core used to clean the task's Camofox
session after every turn. `close_session` only acts if the in-process `_sessions` map still holds the
task, so in practice teardown is best-effort rather than guaranteed — but I did observe one DELETE land
exactly on a turn boundary. If that path ever becomes reliable, an adopted tab could be destroyed
between turns even with this patch, which would bring the original error back for a different reason.
I have not shipped a lifecycle change for that because I cannot test it with the same harness (it needs
real turn boundaries, not separate processes) — flagging it rather than guessing.

Reproduced on macOS with memory-wiki 1.1.0 at official catalog pin `54afaf50`, Hermes 0.22.5. Adding measurements and a locally tested backend fix to this existing issue rather than filing a duplicate.

## Reproduction and scope

A consistent read-only SQLite backup of a local history (2,085 sessions / 57,880 messages) was used; no conversation text, DB, tokens, user paths or memory entries are uploaded here. Both implementations were run in separate loopback-only Uvicorn processes against the same snapshot. The four requests below were launched concurrently; `/ping` is a trivial async endpoint issued 300 ms later. Client socket timeout was 30 s. This is a backend HTTP experiment, not a measurement of the entire Desktop UI or a reproduction of exit 75.

| Request | Unmodified 1.1.0 | Patched |
|---|---:|---:|
| subjects, limit=100 | HTTP 200, 37.848 s | HTTP 200, 12.010 s |
| days, limit=60 | HTTP 200, 37.848 s | HTTP 200, 15.221 s |
| subject detail | HTTP 200, 9.652 s | HTTP 200, 15.775 s |
| overview | socket timeout at 30.001 s | HTTP 200, 16.814 s |
| unrelated async ping during aggregation | socket timeout at 30.002 s | HTTP 200, 0.002 s |

Socket read timeouts are not strict wall-clock deadlines; some responses received headers before their body was delayed, explaining the baseline 37.848 s completions.

## Cause and proposed fix

1. All five installed API handlers are `async def` but call blocking SQLite/CPU aggregation directly, without an await. A burst queues expensive scans on the host event loop and can starve unrelated requests. Use FastAPI's synchronous `def` handlers so the framework dispatches them in its worker pool.
2. The same sessions are repeatedly run through the extraction regexes by overview, subject/day lists and details. Cache the **pure per-session candidate transform** by a SHA-256 digest of its freshly read inputs, not the whole DB/WAL timestamp. This preserves correctness under an active WAL, message edits/deletes/compaction, metadata changes and different profiles: there are no cached query results or raw message strings, and identical inputs alone share identical derived values.
3. Bound the process-local cache (2,048 entries and 500,000 candidates), store frozen candidates and return detached lists; lock concurrent extraction to share work. This is a stopgap, not an indexed/persistent history engine. Python object/string overhead is additional and cold CPU work remains; exceptionally large histories or cache churn may still require indexing or process isolation. No claim that worker threads eliminate all possible GIL starvation.
4. Protect initial dynamic core import with a lock now that routes can execute concurrently. No timeout increase, data truncation or LLM calls.

Sequential backend function measurements on another fresh snapshot: baseline subjects/days/subject-detail/day-detail = 7.942/7.008/8.479/7.021 s; patched = 8.478/1.544/2.523/1.157 s. The initial cold pass is not faster; the improvement is reuse and event-loop responsiveness.

## Verification

- Python tests: **24 passed** (21 existing + 3 regression tests).
- Exact output parity against the untouched baseline for subjects, filtered subjects, days, subject-detail and day-detail on the same snapshot.
- Existing read-only DB/auth integration tests pass.
- New tests exercise cache reuse, edited/deleted message inputs, metadata changes, detached lists, entry/candidate bounds, concurrent single-flight, and all five routes leaving the host event loop responsive.
- `git diff --check` passes. Frontend is unchanged.

Related: #49 already addresses async offloading and subject-search caching. The per-session extraction reuse here also helps overview and day/detail paths while the DB is actively changing. This is a proposed alternative/complement, not a request to merge overlapping changes blindly.

**Symptom:** the Desktop page calls `/subjects?q=&limit=100` and gets `Timed out connecting to Hermes backend after 30000ms` every time. The same gateway process also owns the WhatsApp bridge, so each attempt stalls messaging for ~30 s.

**Where the time goes.** I timed the core functions directly against a read-only copy of the history:

| step | time |
|---|---:|
| `_load_memory_sessions(limit=500)`: DB read, 26,452 messages | 0.9 s |
| `extract_subject_candidates` over those sessions | 25.2 s |
| `build_memory_subjects(limit=100)`, total | 33.6 s |
| `build_daily_logs(limit_days=60)`, total | 28.7 s |

By role, the 500 loaded sessions carry 96.7 MB of `tool` content, 7.7 MB of `user` and 3.6 MB of `assistant`. Nearly all of the regex work runs over tool output.

**Minimal local fix** (applied here, tests green):

1. Do not scan tool-role bodies. Tool *names* still count via `tool_name` and `tool_calls`.
2. Cap every other body at 4,000 characters before the regex and whitespace passes.
3. Make the five routes plain `def`, so FastAPI runs them in the threadpool and they stop blocking the event loop (the same idea as #234).

```python
_MAX_SCAN_CHARS = 4000

def _bounded_content(message: dict) -> str:
    if message.get("role") == "tool":
        return ""
    content = message.get("content")
    if content is None:
        return ""
    return (content if isinstance(content, str) else str(content))[:_MAX_SCAN_CHARS]

def _message_text(message: dict) -> str:
    return " ".join(_bounded_content(message).split())

# extract_subject_candidates: content = _bounded_content(message)
```

I also need the behavior requested in #260: choosing configured model routes and configured profile routes from the same conversation and the same `delegate_task` batch, without changing the active backend between tasks.

## Use case

A coordinator should be able to send a short lookup to a lightweight model route, a difficult analysis to a stronger model route, and a repository task to an existing coding profile, together. Creating a profile for each model-only option adds unnecessary configuration; switching delegation modes prevents the mixed batch.

The desired distinction is **different tasks choose different destination types**. I am not requesting both a model override and a profile on the same task, and I am not requesting execution on another machine as part of this issue.

## Preferred minimal shape

Let one configured route list contain model routes and profile routes, with the same named `option` selector. The following is illustrative, not a claim that current main supports it:

```yaml
delegation:
  backend: model_map
  backends:
    model_map:
      options:
        - name: quick
          description: Short lookups
          provider: example-provider
          model: example-model
        - name: code
          description: Repository work under the coding profile
          profile: coder
```

A single `delegate_task` batch would then choose `option: quick` for one task and `option: code` for another. Each task selects exactly one allowed route. No new backend or core model-override behavior is necessary for this request.

## Acceptance details

- A mixed batch successfully dispatches model-route and profile-route tasks without a mode switch.
- A profile route retains core's existing profile-route semantics, including its configured model and credential scope. Do not imply this also changes toolset or transcript ownership.
- Ambiguous entries combining `profile` with model/provider override fields are rejected explicitly, rather than silently ignoring the override.
- Validation, config display/editing, defaults, and persisted configuration all support both route types; runtime-only pass-through is insufficient.
- Schema enums, descriptions and reported route identity remain accurate; existing model-only and profile-only configurations keep working.

## Existing implementation proposals

PR #273 introduces profile entries in `model_map`. PR #289 also addresses storage/validation/display and rejects a mixed profile-plus-model entry. Those are the relevant existing proposals; I have not independently tested either PR or verified their reported live runs.

Would it be useful to make the mixed-batch acceptance case explicit in #260 and cover it in the selected implementation, rather than opening another feature issue?

I exercised the native Runs API with **two real, isolated gateway processes on loopback**, one serving a named `worker` profile. Inference was a deterministic local test fixture following upstream's daemon-test pattern; gateway admission, profile/session routing and terminal execution were real and unpatched. ```
agent.conversation_loop: API call failed (attempt 1/3) error_type=RuntimeError provider=claude-subscription-directsdk-experimental model=opus summary=Native request failed: error_max_turns
  File ".../directsdk.py", line 1016, in _run
agent.conversation_loop: API call failed (attempt 3/3) ... error_max_turns

## Clarification requested

PR #245 documents successful real Max-subscription requests truthfully identifying as `hermes-agent` on CLI 2.1.316. Our corresponding Team/2.1.318 path is rejected. This does not yet isolate plan tier, account eligibility, CLI version or a changed upstream rule.

- If yes, what supported CLI/account configuration should be used, and can these request IDs be correlated with the rejection?
- Does the Max qualification in #245 have a plan-eligibility limitation that should be stated in the plugin listing?

We are not asking to remove/spoof caller identity, weaken admission, disguise prompts, or enable paid extra usage. Raw conversations, account identifiers and credentials are intentionally omitted.

## Why stamp-based invalidation collapses on active installs

@tillstriegel's PR caches subjects correctly, but the invalidation key is the
database file: `state.db` + `-wal` mtimes with a 5s TTL. On an active install the
gateway writes to *some* session every few seconds, so the stamps keep changing
and the cache keeps resetting — @liiopp measured exactly that above, and we see
the same on a large history. The unit of invalidation shouldn't be the database
file; it should be the session.

## Proposal: per-session units with fingerprint invalidation

The sessions table already carries per-row write markers — `message_count`,
`tool_call_count`, `transcript_revision`, `last_active` — and the gateway bumps
them on every append, rewrite, and rewind. So we memoize each session's
extraction (candidates, snippets, work items, timestamps) as one JSON-serializable
"unit" under a fingerprint of exactly those fields:

- warm requests re-assemble the aggregates from units without reading any
  messages — milliseconds instead of a 40–90 s full scan;
- a write to one session invalidates exactly that session's unit; unrelated
  activity elsewhere never resets anything;
- units persist to an atomic sidecar JSON under `HERMES_HOME/cache/memory-wiki/`
  (profile-scoped), so warm state survives gateway restarts; the store is bounded
  by unit count and serialized size with least-recently-active eviction;
- one process-wide lock lets concurrent cold requests share the same build;
- `MEMORY_WIKI_CACHE=off` restores the uncached path, and `cache=None` (the
  default in the core API) keeps the original behavior — API shapes unchanged.

## Numbers on a real profile (~574 MB, 780 sessions, 29.5k messages)

Measured end-to-end on a cold process against the pre-PR main code, asserting
payload equality at every step:

- pre-PR main: ~76 s per overview request
- cached, cold (first view after deploy): ~65 s
- cached, warm (repeat view, including after a gateway restart): ~5–6 s
- cached after the gateway wrote to one session: ~7 s (only that session re-scanned)

Correctness: the cached payload is identical to the uncached one (asserted in
the tests, equality cold==warm==uncached, plus a real-profile benchmark run
against the pre-PR main code), and every pre-existing test passes.

Same failure here, with a root cause and a fix that has been running on our fleet since 2026-11-09.

Environment: Linux, Claude Code 2.1.306 and 2.1.319 (both behave the same), Opus 5.5, per-call path.

**Cause, confirmed by replaying a real failing request:** the model sends a tool call with invalid JSON. In our case it was `fact_store` with an unquoted list value, the same shape as the `find: show running-config all` example above. `admission.py` `Capture._block_stop` marks the call unparsed, then `Capture._stop` deletes it; the comment there expects only `max_tokens` cutoffs to cause this. The message ends with `stop_reason: tool_use` and zero calls, so `directsdk.py` raises `error_max_turns`. Hermes retries the same context, the model often makes the same mistake again, and after 3 attempts the turn fails. Our diagnostic line: `native_subtype error_max_turns, tool_count 0, upstream_stop_reasons [tool_use], block_types []`.

**Fix we run (local patch to `admission.py` and `directsdk.py`):**
- Drop unparsed calls only when the stop was a length cutoff. When `stop_reason` is `tool_use`, keep the completed call and pass its raw arguments to Hermes. Hermes then returns its normal "invalid JSON" tool result and the model retries.
- When that call is sent back in history, send `input` as an object, e.g. `{"_invalid_arguments": "<raw>"}`. Our first attempt sent the raw string and the API rejected it with HTTP 400, because `tool_use.input` must be an object.

### A tool parked for minutes

Claude Code waits on the parked `tools/call` for `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT` (24 h on a kept process), and Hermes' request timeout and stale timer run only inside `create()`, so a park is not a stall. The one-hour idle timer does run during a park. After an hour the process ends and the next step starts a new one with per-call bytes (`test_idle_eviction_during_a_park_falls_back_to_per_call_bytes`).

A design question, since the timer is this PR's: should a park count as idle? Two small ways out: pause the timer while native waits on a parked call, or add a `session_idle_seconds` setting. We did neither.

## Live run on a claude.ai login: 34 tool rounds with a `/steer` at round 12

The maintainer review asked for a live session with a `/steer` mid-loop and the per-step cache reads against per-call. Here it is, on this branch (`5ca7f23`).

Setup: Hermes v0.23.1 gateway on a Linux machine, Claude Code 2.1.322, a Pro login, Opus 5.5. The task is 34 `terminal` calls, one per step (`echo proof-N`). When the 12th tool call starts, `POST /v1/runs/{run_id}/steer` asks for `echo steered-N` from the next step on. The same script ran three times: kept, per-call (`session_mode: false`), kept again.

| | Kept | Per-call | Kept, second run |
|---|---|---|---|
| The steer | accepted; Hermes delivered it after round 12; steps 13 to 34 ran `steered-N` | the same | the same |
| Claude Code for the 35 model calls | one process, the same pid from the first call to the last, across the steer | a new process per call | one process, the same pid |
| Model call, median (Hermes' log) | 1.0 s | 1.5 s | 1.0 s |
| The call that carries the steer | 1.1 s | 1.7 s | 1.2 s |
| Whole run | 42.9 s | 57.2 s | 41.3 s |
| Cache read, step 1 | 63,284 | 63,284 | 63,284 |
| Cache read, every later step | the previous request less 2 tokens (less 317 at step 2, less 4 after the steer) | the same | the same |
| Tokens written at the steer step | 228 | 228 | 228 |
| Tokens written at a plain round | 89 | 89 | 89 |

So the steer step reads the whole loop from cache in both modes, and the kept process is still the one that started the turn.

What this does not show:
- Equal absolute token counts. The first request was 65,263, 65,325 and 65,330 input tokens in the three runs, in that order: the agent's own context (memory) moved between runs, in both modes. The per-step figures above are the comparison.
- A compaction. This run has none.
- macOS or Windows, or another Claude Code version.

One run per column, so the times are an example, not a measurement. The offline bench in the PR body is the measurement.

## Fail closed: the maintainer review's items 1 to 4

The rule: any doubt about the kept process means kill it and replay per-call bytes on a fresh one; never forward native's version; never wait forever.

**1. `canonical_history()`.** Rows that do not line up were already `HERMES_SESSION_DIVERGED` on this branch. The bare `except ... return payload` is gone too: a body the relay cannot read is a divergence, refused before upstream. New relay test: a resumed request with a row that is not an object. With #361's `return payload` put back, it is forwarded; now it is refused.

**2. The first resumed request.** It is the first with rows Claude Code built itself past its launch's replay, so no earlier request vouches for them. The plugin now builds the request a per-call step sends for the same frames: a one-shot whose relay keeps that request and sends nothing upstream. The kept process's request goes upstream only if it is byte for byte the same. Different: refused, restart (`diverged`), replay. If the per-call request cannot be built: restart (`unproven`). The cost is one per-call launch, once per kept process, at that step. Test: the kept process's record of the first reply differs from what per-call sends (one tool argument, changed after the rows lined up). Before, that request went upstream. Now it is refused and replayed, and every request upstream is per-call's.

**3. `tools/call`.** No `claudecode/toolUseId`: restart (`no_tool_id`). An id the step never received, or one asked before: restart (`tool_id`). Nothing is parked under `None` or an unknown id. Claude Code asks for a tool as soon as its call has streamed, so a doubt can arrive while the answer is still streaming. Before the step's request went upstream, the step replays on a fresh one-shot. After, the answer stands and the process is not kept.

**4. Unknown shapes.** A `control_request` other than the hermes server's MCP traffic: restart (`control`). It is still answered with an error, so a reply already streaming finishes. An output line that is not a JSON object: restart (`event`). The same holds while a new process replays the history: that step runs per-call.

## Version gate and settings in user config (review item 5, "Settings in user config")

**Version gate.** Kept mode runs only on the Claude Code versions the session suite passed on, listed in `plugin.yaml` on the `claude` dependency: `session_versions: [2.1.292, 2.1.322, 2.1.323]` (2.1.292 is the CI pin). Any other version runs every call per-call, with one log line per version:

`claude-subscription-directsdk: session mode runs only on Claude Code 2.1.292, 2.1.322, 2.1.323; this is <version>, so every call runs per-call (a new process each)`

The version is the one each Claude Code process reports in its own stream-json init event (`claude_code_version`). The plugin keeps it per binary, until a file of that binary changes. So no extra process is started to ask, and the first step on a new or updated binary runs per-call. Only a release's own number counts: `2.1.323-beta.1` is not 2.1.323. A kept process ends at its next step when its version leaves the list (restart reason `version`). A Claude Code update then costs latency, never correctness. `evals/ci.sh` runs `tests/test_directsdk_session_version.py` on the pin, so a pin bumped without listing it fails there.

A choice you can change: the list holds exact versions, the three the suite passed on, not a range. A range would also let in versions between them that no test ran.

**Settings.** `session_mode`, `max_sessions` and the new `session_idle_seconds` (default 3600, the prompt cache's lifetime) are read from the serving profile's config on every call (`hermes config set plugins.entries.claude-subscription-directsdk-experimental.settings.<key> <value>`). ## Memory follows the benefit

**A process only where it pays.** A conversation starts a kept process only once it has had `session_min_rounds` tool rounds (default 8; a round is one set of tool results Hermes sends back). Before that every call runs per-call, so short chats and most subagents hold no process. A process kept already meets every later step, and ends there if the history no longer fits it, as after a compaction.

**Eviction at the cap.** At `max_sessions`, the kept process that has waited longest for its user gives its place to the step asking now. One serving a step or holding a parked tool call is never evicted; if every one is, that step runs per-call. Each eviction logs `Claude session evicted` at debug level.

**A parked call is not idle.** The idle limit (`session_idle_seconds`, default 3600, the cache lifetime) counts only while a kept process waits for its user. While Hermes runs a tool, however long, the process stays. It ends at the next step if that step cannot continue it, or when its client closes. Turning `session_mode` off ends a kept process at the next call.

**Subagents.** Stock Hermes already closes a finished child's client: `tools/delegate_tool_child_run.py` calls `child.close()` when the delegate completes; `AIAgent.close` (`run_agent.py`, line 945) closes the shared client and the cached per-request one with `client.close()` (`agent/client_lifecycle.py`, line 204; line numbers at Hermes v0.23.1), and the plugin's `close()` ends the kept process at once. No plugin change was needed. The finalizer for a client dropped without `close()` stays.

**Default** stays on.

**Promised in the last two comments, now pushed.** This push carries what the fail-closed and version-gate comments said would come with the next push:
- What a kept process echoed while the per-call request for its first resumed step was being built is dropped before the step reads (the stale-line window, Grok's finding in the fail-closed comment). No test forces that timing.
- A kept process whose init event names another Claude Code version than the gate allowed is not kept (`version`), so an update in place cannot give one kept step on an unlisted version.
- The README now says a kept process ends at its next step when its binary changes, so also on a move to another listed version.
- The same-size update test: a file replaced (new inode) or rewritten in place (new mtime) counts as a new binary.
Still as those two comments state them: a line that is not JSON at all, after the step's request went upstream, fails the step; the probe's relay is told it is a probe just after its launch; a command naming a file that changes on every run never gets a version and runs per-call without a log line.

The maintainer review asked for one live session on a real claude.ai login, 30+ tool rounds with a compaction and a `/steer` mid-loop, with the per-step cache reads against per-call. This is it, on this branch's head (`fc71f5d`). The live run posted here earlier today (at `5ca7f23`) had no compaction, and that head kept a process from the first call; this one keeps it only after 8 tool rounds.

## macOS, and whether `accept()` can hold the loop

**Can a connection that is gone before it is accepted hold the relay's loop?** The PR's description says `server.timeout = 0` closes the second select only, and that `accept()` itself is as on `main`. To see whether it can wait at all, a probe opens a connection to a blocking listener and resets it (`SO_LINGER` 0, then close) before the server accepts, then checks whether the listener reads as ready and whether `accept()` then waits. It also does the same against a real relay 20 times and checks whether `close()` returns within 3 s.

| | Listener ready after the reset | `accept()` waited over 2 s | Relay `close()` held over 3 s (of 20) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linux 7.0 x86-64, `main` and this branch | yes | no | 0 and 0 |
| macOS 26.6.2 arm64, `main` and this branch | yes | no | 0 and 0 |

On both, `accept()` did not wait for a connection reset before it is accepted (the probe's limit is 2 s), so the wait the Grok review describes did not occur there, and this branch does not make the listener non-blocking.
